analysis.one_liner: Bans sending US natural gas abroad for re-export through foreign LNG terminals, targeting Mexico.
analysis.headline: The bill drew no cosponsors, never got a hearing or vote, and died in committee when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it illegal to export US-produced natural gas to another country with the plan of shipping it onward from that country's LNG export terminal. Its stated purpose, laid out in the findings section, is pressure on Mexico: the bill argues Mexico's corruption, fuel theft, and violations of the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement make routing US gas through Mexican export terminals against US interests. The practical effect would be to force US gas exports to go through terminals located in the United States rather than planned terminals in Mexico.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies that operate US LNG export terminals and gas producers who ship through them, because gas that might have been piped to Mexico and shipped from Mexican terminals would have to flow through US facilities instead. The bill would also give US trade negotiators a pressure point in disputes with Mexico over energy and agricultural commitments.
analysis.who_benefits_short: US LNG terminal operators and gas producers

how_it_helps.text: The bill would prohibit exporting US-produced natural gas to any country with the intent of re-exporting it through a foreign LNG terminal, channeling export business to terminals in the United States.

The findings section frames the ban as a response to Mexican fuel theft, corruption, judicial changes, and energy practices that favor state-owned companies Pemex and the CFE in violation of USMCA commitments.

analysis.who_pays: Mexican power plants, factories, and households that depend on US natural gas, plus US pipeline companies and shippers who send gas across the border, and any US-Mexico trade relationship costs borne by exporters on both sides.
analysis.who_pays_short: Mexican gas buyers and cross-border pipeline shippers

drawbacks.text: The bill would disrupt a large, established US-Mexico gas trade; Mexico relies heavily on US pipeline gas for electricity and industry, and cutting off gas intended for Mexican export terminals would strain that relationship and invite retaliation.

It was a single-sponsor bill with no cosponsors, so it never had the support needed to move, and its narrow focus on foreign re-export terminals would do little for US consumers, since the gas would still be exported, just from US terminals instead.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's main benefit flows to US export terminal operators rather than to American consumers, since it redirects where gas is exported from, not whether it is exported. Its leverage value in trade disputes with Mexico is real but speculative, and the cost would fall largely on Mexican gas buyers and on cross-border pipelines, with some risk of retaliation against US exporters. With zero cosponsors, it was a statement bill rather than a serious legislative effort.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late September 2024 and referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, which never acted on it, and the bill died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Dan Sullivan introduced the bill on September 25, 2024, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources.
No cosponsors signed on to the bill.
The committee took no further action, and the bill received no floor vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mexican gas importers, cross-border pipeline shippers, and developers of Mexican LNG terminals, since the existing US-Mexico gas trade was left untouched; US consumers saw no change either way.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Mexican gas buyers and pipeline shippers

for.name: Sen. Dan Sullivan
for.role: US Senator from Alaska; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban re-exports of US natural gas through foreign LNG terminals and referred to Mexico's corruption and USMCA violations as justification.

against.name: Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on September 25, 2024, and took no further action; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: There was no meaningful test of party support: the bill had a single Republican sponsor, no cosponsors of either party, and never reached a vote.

industries.industry: US LNG export terminals and gas producers
industries.note: The bill would force gas that might have been piped to Mexico and shipped from Mexican terminals to instead flow through US export facilities, protecting US terminal throughput. Exporting gas to world markets tends to raise domestic prices, so the industry's gain here does not flow to American households.

industries.industry: Cross-border pipelines and US gas shippers to Mexico
industries.note: A ban on gas destined for foreign LNG terminals would hit US companies that pipe gas to Mexico, including volumes bound for planned Mexican export projects. Some of those same companies supply Mexican power plants and factories that depend on US gas.

industries.industry: Mexican LNG terminal developers and Mexican gas utilities
industries.note: The bill directly targets terminals in Mexico, cutting off the US gas supply that planned Mexican export projects and Mexican consumers rely on. Mexican households and businesses would bear higher costs or supply risk.
